title_en: Wangari Maathai: The Woman Who Planted a Movement
title_ru: Вангари Маатаи: женщина, посадившая целое движение
description_ru: История кенийской учёной и активистки, которая начала с семи саженцев и получила Нобелевскую премию мира.
text:
When Wangari Maathai was a child in the highlands of Kenya, she used to fetch water from a stream near her family's home. She remembered the clear, cold water, the green ferns along the bank and the frog eggs that looked like beads in the shallows. Decades later she returned to the same place and found that the stream had dried up. The fig trees had been cut down, and the land around it had been turned into fields. That moment helped to inspire a movement that would plant tens of millions of trees across Africa.

Wangari was born in 1940 in the village of Ihithe, near Nyeri. Her parents were farmers, and unlike most girls in her community, she was sent to school, mainly because her older brother insisted. She was an excellent student, and in 1960 she was selected to study in the United States on a scholarship. She earned a degree in biology in Kansas and a master's degree in Pittsburgh, and she later told interviewers that it was there that she first noticed how closely the health of the environment was connected to people's lives.

Back in Kenya, she continued her studies at the University of Nairobi. In 1971 she became the first woman in East and Central Africa to receive a doctorate, and she later became the head of a university department, another first for a woman. She was not always welcome in the male-dominated academic world. Colleagues are said to have laughed when she applied for equal pay and benefits, and she was told more than once that a woman should know her place. She refused to be discouraged.

In the 1970s she began to meet rural women, who told her that their rivers were dirty, their firewood was running out and their children were badly fed. The women had to walk for hours to find fuel, and the soil, washed away by rain, no longer gave good harvests. Wangari's answer was disarmingly simple: plant trees. In 1977 she founded the Green Belt Movement. The women were given seedlings and a small payment for each tree that survived, which meant that planting was not only good for the land but also for their families' budgets.

The first tree nursery was started at her home, and the first planting took place on World Environment Day in 1977, when seven trees were planted in her own backyard. From these humble beginnings, the movement grew, and tens of thousands of women learned to grow trees, to keep records, and to speak in public. By the time Wangari died, it is estimated that more than fifty million trees had been planted in Kenya alone. She often said that a tree was a symbol of peace and hope, and that planting one was an act of defiance against despair.

Planting trees soon brought her into conflict with the powerful. In 1989 the government of President Daniel arap Moi announced plans to build a sixty-storey office tower in Uhuru Park, the largest green space in central Nairobi. Wangari wrote letters, gave interviews and stood in front of the cameras to protest. She was called a madwoman by government ministers, and she was threatened and arrested more than once. During one demonstration in 1992 she was beaten unconscious by police. The investors withdrew, and the park was saved.

Her courage made her famous abroad, and when democracy finally arrived in Kenya, she was elected to parliament in 2002 with an overwhelming majority. She was soon appointed assistant minister for the environment. In 2004 she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, the first African woman to receive it. The committee explained that she had linked sustainable development, democracy and peace. During the ceremony in Oslo she told the audience that, in the course of history, there comes a time when humanity is called to shift to a new level of consciousness.

Wangari told a story that she loved to repeat. A huge forest was on fire, and all the animals ran away in terror. Only a tiny hummingbird flew back and forth to the river, carrying a single drop of water in its beak. The other animals laughed at it and asked what it could possibly achieve. The hummingbird replied that it was doing the best it could. Wangari said that this was exactly what she tried to do, and that everyone could be a hummingbird.

She died of cancer in Nairobi in September 2011, at the age of seventy-one. Thousands of people attended her funeral, and she was buried in a simple coffin made of bamboo and water hyacinth, as she had requested, so that no tree would have to be cut down. Her autobiography is called Unbowed, a fitting title for a woman who was never broken by threats or ridicule. The trees she planted continue to grow, and so does the idea that an ordinary person with a spade can change the world.

questions.question: What did Wangari Maathai see when she returned to the stream of her childhood?
questions.answer: It had dried up and the trees around it had been cut down.

questions.question: How did the Green Belt Movement help women?
questions.answer: They received seedlings and a small payment for each tree that survived.

questions.question: Why did she protest in Uhuru Park?
questions.answer: The government wanted to build a huge office tower in the biggest green space in Nairobi.

questions.question: What did the hummingbird story teach?
questions.answer: Everyone should do the best they can, even if it seems small.
